newsitem.title: UK: INTERVIEW - Willis sceptical about mergers.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Willis sceptical about mergers.

text.p: Significant overcapacity in all lines of business is continuing to pressure pricing in the insurance industry Willis Corroon Group Plc, the international insurance broker said on Thursday.

But despite the difficult market conditions, the company remains sceptical about the benefits of the recent industry trend of pursuing cost economies through mergers group executive director Max Taylor told Reuters.
"Everbody seems to be coming up with every conceivable combination of companies. We still remain sceptical about the benefits of scale for the sake of it," said Taylor.

"We think there are huge risks in people businessses associated with that. We have a strategy for growing our business that we're comfortable with and as far as we're concerned that's what we're concentrating on." Taylor was speaking after the group unveiled a rise in 1996 pre-tax profits to 91.6 million pounds.

Despite difficult market conditions and adverse impact of sterling's recent strength the group had managed to grow the top-line. "We have grown revenues, albeit by only three percent but...in current market circumstances we think that's pretty good," said Taylor. "But it is a fact of life - pricing is extremely competitive in all markets and continues to be so."

The focus going foward was to grow revenue by building market share through the company's change programme by understanding customers' needs more effectively and by developing new products and services.

"Our business is not purely driven by constantly reducing our cost base even though that's something we're doing. We have focused on revenue. The other element is concentrating on delivering our services at the lowest price consistent with high quality service," said Taylor.

After severance costs of 11.3 million pounds in the 1996 figures related to the change programme, Taylor said he expected further costs in 1997 to be lower and again to be taken as ongoing operating expenses.
He said he expected the costs to have pretty swift paybacks of between 12 and 15 months.
After a fall in staff numbers of 11 percent to 9,116 in 1996, further reductions were also expected to be on a smaller scale.

"We had a fairly substantial headcount reduction toward the latter part of 1996 which was quite specific. Over time we need to constantly improve our productivity. From here on in, it is likely that we'll be able to absorb any reduction in headcount through natural turnover or redeployment," said Taylor

The change programme is expected to span three to five years and last year's actions were taken to underpin it. The real effort would now be going into the longer term effort of building capabilities, skills and resources, said Taylor.
